newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsica separatists claim bomb, Juppe vows action.
newsitem.headline: Corsica separatists claim bomb, Juppe vows action.

text.p: Corsican separatists claimed responsibility on Monday for a bomb attack on Prime Minister Alain Juppe's mayoral office in Bordeaux, and an angry government vowed to put the guerrillas out of action.
The "historic wing" of the outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC) said it had planted the bomb on Saturday night, raising the spectre of an offensive in mainland France.

A one-sentence claim sent to news organisations offered no explanation, but the FLNC has accused Juppe of going back on pledges made in secret peace talks earlier this year when he ordered a crackdown on separatist gunmen in July.

Juppe held a 90-minute meeting on the crisis with President Jacques Chirac and said afterwards: "We will not allow a handful of desperados to block the process of solidarity towards Corsica...and re-establishment of authority there."

"Extremely strict orders have been given...that delinquents and criminals be identified, arrested and tried with all the rigours of the law," said Juppe who ordered increased security at public buildings in Paris and provincial cities.

"The government is determined to combat terrorism in all its forms in Corsica...with the same determination it showed last year when our country faced other terrorist violence," Juppe's office also said in a statement, referring to a wave of bombings blamed on, and claimed by, Algerian Moslem fundamentalists that killed eight people and injured 170.
A nationwide security operation, known as "Vigipirate", has been in force since last year's Algeria-linked bombings, but the interior ministry reduced the level of alert in January.
The Bordeaux blast was an escalation of the FLNC's long-running, low-intensity struggle for greater autonomy from Paris.
Juppe's office said that, by placing bombs in Bordeaux on Saturday and in Aix-en-Provence last month, the "historic wing" had turned its back on a dialogue offered by the government.

The FLNC, estimated to have a few hundred armed followers, has long been taken less seriously than the Irish Republican Army (IRA) fighting British rule in Northern Ireland or Basque ETA guerrillas in Spain because it has confined its actions to Corsica and rarely spilled blood.
There have been more than 80 bomb attacks on government offices and police stations in Corsica since July, but Saturday's was only the second for many years on the mainland.
The FLNC has scant popular support and its action has often seemed more theatrical than lethal, on the borderline between politics and organised crime.
Corsican parliamentarians, who are mostly opposed to the separatist cause, hailed Juppe's statements, saying the government's intended action was long overdue.

Juppe ordered the crackdown in July after all parties had accused Paris of being soft on the separatists' 20-year-old bombing campaign and of allowing gunmen to roam the lawless island unchecked and engage in tit-for-tat sectarian killings.
Several suspects have since been detained. The interior ministry announced the arrest of two more suspects in southern Corsica on Monday after police seized a weapons cache.
The opposition Socialists condemned the Bordeaux bombing but said the government had brought the violence upon itself.
"It long conducted secret talks with secret groups and today it seems to be paying a high price since nothing came from the talks," Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande said.
